opts: Stateful inspection of connection tables only
Signature-based detection of known attack strings
Static packet filtering by source address
Anomaly-based detection against a learned baseline
why: Baseline comparison can flag unknown behaviour at the cost of false positives. Signatures detect only what is already known, and stateful inspection and static filters enforce rules without detecting novel attacks.

q: After a breach of one web server, the attacker moved to the database and domain controllers over the flat internal network. Which design change MOST directly limits this lateral movement?
opts: Longer retention of the web server's access logs
Doubling the bandwidth of the core network links
Adding a second internet service provider for failover
Micro-segmentation with default-deny rules between workloads
why: Workload-level segmentation blocks unneeded east-west traffic so one compromise cannot spread freely. Bandwidth, a second ISP and longer logs do not stop movement between internal systems.

q: A company wants to stop staff from emailing files that contain customer card numbers to outside addresses. Which control BEST fits?
opts: Data loss prevention rules that inspect and block content leaving by email
A proxy that caches popular web pages for speed
A load balancer in front of the outbound mail relay
Network access control that checks device patch levels at login
why: DLP inspects content for patterns such as card numbers and blocks or flags the transfer. NAC checks devices, a load balancer spreads traffic and a caching proxy improves performance without examining content for sensitive data.

q: Visitors plug laptops into meeting-room network sockets. The company wants only managed, compliant devices to get access to the internal network. Which control fits BEST?
opts: A content delivery network for the company website
A web application firewall on the intranet portal
A traffic-shaping policy that favours voice traffic
Network access control with 802.1X and a posture check
why: NAC with 802.1X authenticates the device and can check its health before granting access. A WAF protects a web application, a CDN serves public content and traffic shaping manages bandwidth.

q: A small branch office wants one box that provides firewalling, intrusion prevention, web filtering and VPN with a single management console. Which product type is described?
opts: A unified threat management appliance
A thin client for virtual desktops
A hardware security module
A network tap for passive monitoring
why: UTM bundles several security functions for simple management at smaller sites. An HSM protects keys, a tap copies traffic for sensors and a thin client displays a remote desktop.

q: An organization wants to hide its web servers' addresses, offload TLS and filter requests before they reach the application servers. Which device type fits?
opts: A passive IDS sensor connected to a span port
A reverse proxy or web application firewall in front of the servers
A switch with port security enabled on its access ports
A forward proxy that employees use to browse the internet
why: A reverse proxy sits in front of servers, terminates TLS and filters inbound requests. A forward proxy represents clients, a passive sensor cannot filter and port security protects switch ports from rogue devices.

q: An intrusion prevention system is placed on a span port of a core switch, and the security team finds it does not block a confirmed attack. What is the MOST likely reason?
opts: The span port encrypts the traffic so that it cannot be examined
Span ports always block traffic that matches an alert rule
It sees only a copy of the traffic, and blocking needs an inline placement
It has run out of signatures for the attack's file extension
why: A span port provides a passive copy, so the device can alert but not stop the original traffic unless it sits in line. The signature, encryption and blocking explanations do not fit how span ports work.

q: Which TWO statements about intrusion detection methods are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: Signature-based detection finds unknown attacks as well as known ones
Neither method needs any tuning after installation
Anomaly-based detection never produces false positives
Signature-based detection is accurate for known attacks but misses new ones
Anomaly-based detection can find new attacks but produces more false positives
why: Each method has a trade-off: signatures are precise but limited to known patterns, and baselines are broader but noisier. Neither is free of errors and both need ongoing tuning.

q: Micro-segmentation applies policy between individual workloads and helps limit lateral movement.
opts: True
False
why: Workload-level rules mean a compromised system can reach only the flows that its application needs.

q: A unified threat management appliance is usually the best choice for a large data center because it combines every function in one box.
opts: True
False
why: UTM suits smaller sites. Large environments use specialized, scalable layers and avoid a single point of failure and shared performance limits.

q: A network intrusion detection sensor cannot read the content of encrypted traffic unless it is decrypted first or inspected at an endpoint.
opts: True
False
why: Encryption hides the payload from a sensor on the wire, so organizations decrypt at a gateway, inspect on the host, or fall back on metadata and behaviour.

q: An email client is configured to retrieve mail from the server on TCP port 143 with no TLS. Which change BEST protects the credentials and messages?
opts: Keep port 143 and ask users to choose longer mailbox passwords
Change the client to use POP3 on port 110, because it is a simpler protocol
Move the cleartext IMAP service to a higher, less well-known port number
Use IMAP over TLS on port 993, or require STARTTLS, and disable cleartext logins
why: IMAP over TLS (port 993) or an enforced upgrade protects both credentials and content in transit. POP3 on port 110 is also cleartext, a different port number is only obscurity and longer passwords still cross the network readable.

q: A user opens an email attachment and, within minutes, the same malware appears on several other computers on the network without anyone else opening anything. Which malware type is this?
opts: Virus
Trojan
Worm
Logic bomb
why: A worm propagates on its own across a network. A virus requires a host file and user action to spread, a trojan masquerades as legitimate software and does not self-propagate, and a logic bomb triggers on a condition.

q: Antivirus reports nothing, but an EDR alert shows that PowerShell launched from a Word document is downloading and running code in memory. Which classification BEST fits?
opts: A boot sector virus that infects the startup area of the disk
A hardware implant installed in the laptop during manufacture
Fileless malware using living-off-the-land techniques
A macro-free harmless administrative script
why: Running in memory and abusing built-in tools describes fileless, living-off-the-land activity, which signature scanners often miss. A boot sector virus infects the startup area, an administrative script launched from a document is not harmless, and nothing suggests hardware tampering.

q: An organization wants the strongest protection against unknown executables on servers that rarely change. Which control is MOST appropriate?
opts: Increasing the screen lock timeout
A signature-based blocklist
Disabling the host firewall
Application allowlisting
why: Only approved applications run under allowlisting, which suits stable servers. Blocklists stop only known bad software, and the other options either do nothing for execution control or reduce security.

q: A company discovers hundreds of laptops with different, often outdated configurations. Which action BEST establishes a consistent secure posture?
opts: Rely on antivirus software alone to keep laptops secure
Let each user configure their own laptop to suit their work, and record the settings in a shared spreadsheet
Disable all logging on the laptops to improve performance
Define a hardened baseline, deploy it with configuration management and monitor for drift
why: A baseline enforced and checked by tooling creates consistency and detects deviation. User-managed configurations are inconsistent, antivirus alone does not harden, and disabling logging reduces visibility.

q: A lost laptop contained unencrypted customer data. Which control would have BEST reduced the impact?
opts: A longer account lockout threshold on laptop logins
A larger hard drive with more free space
Full-disk encryption with the key protected by a TPM and authentication
A screen saver with a password that locks the laptop after five minutes of inactivity
why: Full-disk encryption protects data at rest on a lost device. Lockout settings and screen savers do not protect the drive when it is removed or booted elsewhere, and drive capacity is irrelevant.

q: An employee uses a personal phone to access corporate email. The company wants to be able to remove only corporate data if the employee leaves. Which solution BEST meets this need?
opts: MDM or UEM with a managed container and selective wipe
A full factory reset of the personal phone
Requiring employees to forward all email to a personal account
Blocking the phone from the network and issuing nothing
why: A managed work container with selective wipe separates corporate and personal data. A full factory reset destroys personal data and is rarely acceptable on a personal device. Forwarding to personal accounts loses control, and blocking provides no access solution.

q: A company moves a customer database from its own servers to an infrastructure-as-a-service virtual machine. Who is responsible for patching the guest operating system?
opts: Both share this equally in every case
The customer
The cloud provider
The hypervisor vendor
why: In IaaS the provider secures the physical infrastructure and virtualization layer while the customer manages the guest operating system, applications and data. The provider patches the OS in PaaS and SaaS, the responsibility is not equally shared here, and the hypervisor vendor is not involved in the tenant's guest.

q: A security review finds that a cloud storage bucket holding customer records is publicly readable because of a permissive policy. According to the shared responsibility model, who is MOST likely accountable for the exposure?
opts: The internet service provider that carries the traffic
The customer, for misconfiguring access to its own data
The end users whose records are stored in the bucket
The cloud provider, for hosting the bucket
why: Customers control configuration of their own resources and data, and misconfiguration is the leading cause of cloud exposure. The provider secures the underlying service but does not own the customer's policy decisions, and neither end users nor ISPs configured the bucket.

q: An organization discovers staff using unapproved SaaS file-sharing services to send sensitive documents. Which technology BEST provides visibility and policy enforcement over this activity?
opts: A cloud access security broker
A hardware security module
A network time server
A Type 1 hypervisor
why: A CASB discovers shadow IT and applies data and access policies to cloud service use. A hypervisor, HSM and time server serve unrelated purposes.

q: Several development virtual machines created for a past project have never been patched and nobody remembers who owns them. Which problem does this describe?
opts: Container breakout
VM escape
Hypervisor type confusion
VM sprawl
why: Uncontrolled growth of unmanaged virtual machines is VM sprawl and is addressed with inventory, ownership and lifecycle management. VM escape is an attack that breaks guest isolation, and the other terms do not describe unmanaged machines.

q: A team runs many containers on one host. Which practice BEST reduces risk from a vulnerable application inside a container?
opts: Run every container as root so that debugging, package installs and file access are easier
Run containers as non-root from minimal, scanned images with restricted capabilities
Disable host logging to save disk space on busy nodes
Store database passwords in the container image so deployments are simple
why: Least privilege, small scanned images and restricted capabilities limit what a compromised container can do. Running as root, embedding secrets in images and disabling logging each increase risk.

q: A web application builds SQL queries by concatenating user input into the statement. Which control MOST directly prevents SQL injection?
opts: Parameterized queries with input validation
A longer session timeout for logged-in users
Output encoding of HTML in the page templates
Encrypting the database backups before they leave the data centre
why: Parameterized queries keep data separate from code so input cannot change the query structure. HTML output encoding addresses cross-site scripting, session timeout concerns session management, and backup encryption protects stored copies rather than live queries.

q: An attacker posts a comment containing a script on a forum, and the script runs in the browsers of other users who view the page. Which attack and primary defence is this?
opts: Cross-site request forgery, defended by longer passwords
Buffer overflow, defended by tightening host firewall rules
Cross-site scripting, defended by output encoding and content security policy
SQL injection, defended by parameterized queries and stored procedures in the database layer
why: Script that runs in other users' browsers is cross-site scripting, prevented by encoding output and restricting script sources. SQL injection targets the database, cross-site request forgery abuses an authenticated session and is mitigated with anti-forgery tokens, and buffer overflow is a memory corruption problem.

q: A company receives complaints that fraudulent emails appear to come from its domain. Which combination of controls MOST directly lets receivers verify and reject spoofed mail?
opts: SPF, DKIM and a DMARC policy
Full-disk encryption on mail servers
A stronger firewall password
An internal certificate authority
why: SPF and DKIM authenticate the sending infrastructure and message, and DMARC tells receivers what to do on failure. Firewall passwords, disk encryption and an internal CA do not authenticate mail for external receivers.

q: Which TWO controls MOST directly help defend endpoints against fileless malware? (Choose two.)
opts: Relying only on weekly signature updates
Endpoint detection and response with behaviour monitoring
Disabling the host firewall
Longer password expiration intervals
Script logging and constrained use of PowerShell
why: Fileless attacks abuse legitimate tools, so behaviour monitoring and script control are effective. Signature-only approaches miss them, and the firewall and password settings do not address in-memory execution.

q: Which TWO statements about the cloud shared responsibility model are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: The customer is always responsible for its own data and access configuration
Moving to the cloud transfers all legal accountability to the provider
In IaaS the provider patches the customer's guest operating system
In SaaS the provider manages more of the stack than in IaaS
The provider is responsible for the customer's identity policies
why: Customers keep responsibility for data, identities and configuration, and the provider's share grows from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS. In IaaS the customer patches the guest OS, legal accountability for data remains with the customer, and identity policy is a customer configuration.

q: Which TWO measures reduce the risk of a hypervisor compromise affecting every guest? (Choose two.)
opts: Isolate hypervisor management interfaces on a dedicated management network
Disable logging on the host
Patch the hypervisor promptly
Expose the management interface to the internet for convenience
Run all guests with the same root password
why: Timely patching and isolated management reduce exposure of the component that all guests depend on. Internet exposure, shared passwords and disabling logs each increase the risk.

q: A web application team is improving secure development practices. Which TWO activities BEST support a secure software development lifecycle? (Choose two.)
opts: Threat modelling during design
Letting developers push straight to production without review
Automated static and dynamic security testing in the build pipeline
Adding security controls only after release
Using the same credentials for all environments
why: Security belongs at the start through threat modelling and continues through automated testing. Retrofitting after release is costly, bypassing review removes a safeguard, and sharing credentials across environments enlarges the blast radius of any leak.

q: In a platform-as-a-service deployment the provider patches the underlying operating system, while the customer stays responsible for its own application code and data.
opts: True
False
why: In PaaS the provider runs the infrastructure, operating system and runtime. The customer secures the application, its configuration, identities and data.

q: Containers share the host operating system kernel, so a kernel vulnerability can affect all containers on that host.
opts: True
False
why: Containers are lighter than virtual machines because they share the kernel, which also reduces isolation.

q: Application allowlisting only blocks software that is already known to be malicious.
opts: True
False
why: That describes blocklisting. Allowlisting permits only approved applications and blocks everything else by default.

q: Cross-site scripting is best prevented with parameterized database queries.
opts: True
False
why: Parameterized queries prevent SQL injection. Cross-site scripting is mitigated by output encoding, input validation and content security policy.

q: A cloud access security broker can help an organization discover and control the use of unapproved cloud applications.
opts: True
False
why: CASBs provide visibility into shadow IT and enforce data protection and access policy on cloud services.

q: A technician finds that security tools on a server report nothing, yet the machine behaves oddly and network traffic shows connections to an unknown address. A scan run from a rescue disk reveals a hidden driver. What does this MOST likely indicate?
opts: A logic bomb that has not yet reached the date on which it is set to run but is already making connections
A macro virus that has infected only documents stored on one file share
A rootkit that hides itself from tools running inside the compromised operating system
A scareware program that is displaying pop-up warnings to scare the user
why: Hidden components that only show up when the system is examined from outside are typical of a rootkit, which tampers with what the running operating system reports. Scareware is visible by design, a macro virus lives in documents and a dormant logic bomb would not be making network connections.

q: A free screen-saver program installs normally, then quietly opens a hidden remote connection for an attacker. How is this program BEST classified?
opts: A trojan, because it hides a harmful function inside software that looks useful
A trapdoor, because it was written by the developers of the operating system
A worm, because it opened a connection over the network to another system
A boot-sector virus, because it was installed and runs after the system starts
why: A trojan looks legitimate while carrying a hidden function, and does not replicate itself. A worm copies itself across networks on its own, a boot-sector virus infects the startup area, and a trapdoor is an undocumented entry left by a developer in their own code.

q: A worm that exploits an unpatched file-sharing service is spreading between servers in a data center. Which action MOST directly limits the spread?
opts: Train staff not to open attachments from unknown senders
Encrypt the disks of all servers so that the worm cannot read the files
Patch the vulnerable service and block it between network segments
Require longer passwords for every administrator account in the data center
why: A worm spreads by itself through a vulnerable network service, so patching that service and blocking it between segments stops the spread. Longer passwords, disk encryption and attachment training do not address self-propagation through an exposed service.

q: A developer checks that a file is safe to open and then opens it, but an attacker swaps the file in the short gap between the two steps. Which weakness is this?
opts: A race condition of the time of check to time of use type
A buffer overflow caused by missing bounds checking of the input
SQL injection caused by concatenating text into a database query
Cross-site scripting caused by unencoded output in a web page
why: When the state changes between a check and the later use, the result is a race condition, specifically time of check to time of use. A buffer overflow writes past a memory boundary, and the injection and scripting flaws involve untrusted input interpreted as commands or markup.

q: A web page the staff routinely read for industry news is compromised and silently installs malware on visitors' laptops. Which attack is this?
opts: A distributed denial of service attack against the publisher
A watering-hole attack that uses a drive-by download
A smishing campaign sent by text message to company phones
A spear-phishing campaign that targets a single named executive
why: Compromising a site that a target group is known to visit, so that visitors are infected, is a watering-hole attack, and the silent install is a drive-by download. Phishing and smishing deliver lures by email or text, and a denial of service aims to make the site unavailable.

q: An attacker's page makes a logged-in user's browser send a request to the bank's transfer function without the user noticing. Which defence is MOST effective against this?
opts: Parameterized queries in the database layer behind the transfer function
Anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies on the application's sensitive requests
Full-disk encryption on the bank's application servers
A longer minimum password length for all of the bank's customers
why: A forged cross-site request succeeds because the browser attaches the session automatically, so unpredictable per-request tokens and SameSite cookies block it. Parameterized queries stop injection, password length does not affect an authenticated session, and disk encryption protects data at rest.

q: A finance manager receives a text message that appears to come from the bank, stating that the account will be frozen unless a link is opened within an hour. What is this attack, and what is the BEST response?
opts: Vishing; call back the number shown in the message to check it quickly
Spam; ignore it, because unwanted bulk messages are not harmful
Whaling; reply to the sender to confirm that the account is genuine
Smishing; do not use the link and contact the bank through a known number
why: A text-message lure is smishing, and the urgency is a pressure tactic, so the safe move is to use an independently known contact route. Vishing uses voice calls, replying or calling back through the supplied details stays inside the attacker's channel, and treating it as harmless spam ignores the credential-theft risk.

q: An analyst reviews a user account that normally downloads a few files a day but has just copied 40 GB from the engineering share at 3 a.m. from a new location. Which type of tool is MOST likely to flag this automatically?
opts: A signature-based antivirus scanner on the user's laptop
A hardware security module in the data center
User and entity behaviour analytics that compares activity with a baseline
A static application security testing tool in the build pipeline
why: Behaviour analytics learns what is normal for each user and raises alerts on deviations such as unusual volume, time and place. An antivirus scanner looks for known malware, an HSM protects keys and a static testing tool inspects source code before release.

q: A critical security patch has been released for software on production servers, and the business can accept only a short maintenance window. Which approach BEST balances speed and safety?
opts: Install it only on the servers whose owners ask for it, and skip any check that it worked
Deploy it to every production server at once without any testing, because the flaw is rated critical
Test it on a pilot group or staging copy, deploy it in the window with a rollback plan, and verify the result afterwards
Delay it until the next quarterly maintenance cycle, so that it is bundled with other changes
why: Even an urgent patch is tested on a small group first, deployed in a planned window with a way back, and verified afterwards. Untested mass deployment risks outages, waiting a quarter leaves a critical flaw open, and patching only on request without verification leaves gaps and gives no proof that the fix worked.

q: A security manager asks why a host-based intrusion detection system is still useful when a network sensor already monitors all traffic. Which answer is MOST accurate?
opts: It sees activity on the host, such as file changes and processes, including inside encrypted sessions
It replaces the need for patching, because it can fix the flaws it discovers on every host it monitors
It blocks all outside traffic before it can reach the host
It only works when the host is connected to the corporate network
why: A host agent observes local behaviour and decrypted content that a network sensor cannot see. It detects rather than patches, works offline because it runs on the host, and a detection system that does not block is not a firewall.

q: Laptops of remote workers connect to hotel and cafe networks, and the company worries about attacks between devices on the same network. Which control MOST directly addresses this?
opts: A faster internet connection for the head office
A perimeter firewall at the company head office network edge
Link aggregation on the head office core switches
A host-based firewall with default-deny inbound rules enforced centrally
why: Only a firewall running on the laptop protects it when it is on a network the company does not control. The head office firewall and switches are not in the path, and a faster connection does not change the exposure.

q: An organization needs to hold the signing keys of its internal certificate authority so that no administrator can ever extract them, and use of the keys needs two of five officers. Which technology fits BEST?
opts: An encrypted file on a protected network share
A password manager shared by the five administrators
The TPM chip of the administrator's own laptop
A hardware security module with quorum authentication
why: An HSM keeps private keys inside tamper-resistant hardware and can require an M of N quorum for sensitive actions. A shared password manager and a file share expose the key material, and a laptop TPM protects only that one device and does not provide a shared, quorum-controlled service.

q: Device management reports that an employee's personal phone, which has corporate email installed, has been rooted. Which response BEST protects corporate data?
opts: Allow access as before, because the owner is a trusted employee and the phone is personally owned
Mark the device non-compliant and block its access to corporate apps until it is restored
Erase the whole phone at once, including the owner's personal photos and messages
Rely on the phone's own antivirus app to clean the device and leave access unchanged
why: Root or jailbreak access can bypass the platform protections that keep corporate data separate, so compliance policy treats the device as non-compliant and blocks corporate access until it is fixed. Granting access ignores the risk, a full erase overreaches on a personal device, and an app running on a compromised platform cannot be trusted to clean it.

q: The company wants to manage and wipe only its own apps on staff-owned phones, without enrolling the whole device. Which capability is described?
opts: A corporate-owned, business-only device provisioning model
Mobile application management with per-app policies and selective wipe
A full mobile device management enrolment with supervised mode
A network access control check at the guest wireless network
why: MAM controls apps and their data directly, which suits BYOD. Full device management and corporate-owned models give control over the entire device, and a network check does not manage apps or data.

q: After a ransomware alert on a workstation, the EDR console offers several actions. Which is the BEST first containment action while keeping the evidence available to responders?
opts: Delete the suspicious file and close the alert as resolved
Reimage the workstation from the standard corporate build
Power off the workstation by holding the power button down
Isolate the host from the network through the EDR agent
why: Network isolation stops spread and communication with the attacker while memory and disk stay intact and the agent can still be reached. Powering off loses volatile data, reimaging destroys evidence and removing one file without analysis leaves the cause unknown.

q: A security team has no alerts but suspects that a skilled attacker is present, because a partner has reported that attackers used a technique that is not covered by current detection rules. What is the BEST next step?
opts: Wait for automated alerts to fire before taking any action
Run a hypothesis-driven threat hunt for that technique in the stored telemetry
Ask the partner to run a vulnerability scan against the company network
Disable the least-reliable detection rules to reduce analyst workload
why: Threat hunting searches for what automated detection missed, using intelligence about attacker techniques. Waiting leaves a possible intruder in place, disabling rules reduces coverage and a partner's scan does not look for an intruder.

q: Several hospitals share one cloud environment built to meet the same health-sector regulations and run by a joint committee. Which deployment model is this?
opts: Hybrid cloud
Community cloud
Private cloud
Public cloud
why: A community cloud is shared by organizations with common requirements. A public cloud is open to the general public, a hybrid cloud combines two or more models, and a private cloud serves a single organization.

q: A cloud customer needs an isolated network section with its own address range, subnets and firewall rules inside a public provider. Which construct provides this?
opts: A content delivery network
A physical air gap
A community cloud
A virtual private cloud
why: A VPC is a logically isolated network in a public cloud that the customer designs and controls. A community cloud is a sharing model, a CDN distributes content and an air gap cannot exist inside a shared public provider.

q: The company has issued a legal hold after being notified of a lawsuit. The emails it must produce sit in a SaaS service across several regions. What should the security team do NEXT?
opts: Ask employees to forward the relevant emails to personal accounts so that they can be collected quickly
Let the provider's retention policy age out older mailboxes automatically, so that less data has to be produced
Export every mailbox into an unprotected shared folder for the lawyers
Work with the provider to preserve and export the relevant mailboxes with their metadata, and keep custody records
why: After the hold, the data must be collected defensibly, which in a multi-region SaaS service needs the provider's help to preserve and export it in usable formats with metadata, with custody documented. Letting retention delete data after a hold is spoliation, and an unprotected folder or personal accounts break custody and confidentiality.

q: A company is selecting a cloud provider for payroll data. Which contract term MOST reduces the risk of being locked in and left with undeleted data at the end?
opts: A very high uptime percentage in the service-level agreement
A marketing commitment to share product news with staff regularly
A discount that applies to a long multi-year commitment to the provider and rises with every extra year signed
Defined data export formats, exit assistance and certified destruction at termination
why: Portability, exit support and destruction terms address the end of the relationship directly. An uptime figure covers availability, marketing commitments are not security terms and discounts for long commitments increase lock-in.

q: A cloud provider suffers an outage in one region and a customer that runs only in that region loses its service. The customer assumed the provider's redundancy covered everything. Which lesson applies?
opts: The provider is always fully liable for any customer outage under the shared responsibility model
Encryption keys should be kept in the same region as the workloads
Resilience such as multi-zone design and tested backups remains the customer's responsibility
Backups are unnecessary when a provider operates several data centres
why: Under shared responsibility the customer designs for availability and recovery on top of the provider's platform, including backups and multi-zone or multi-region deployment. A provider is not liable for design choices, backups remain necessary and key location does not address an outage.

q: A firewall delivered as a prebuilt virtual machine image was downloaded from a forum and deployed in production. What is the MOST important risk?
opts: The image will use more storage than a physical firewall
Virtual appliances are always faster than physical hardware
Virtual appliances cannot inspect any network traffic at all, because they run inside a hypervisor
The image may contain malware or backdoors, so its source and integrity must be verified
why: Unverified images are a supply chain risk, so obtain them from the vendor and check hashes or signatures, then harden. Virtual appliances can inspect traffic routed through them, and storage use and speed are not the central security concern.

q: An administrator keeps a snapshot of a production database server for six months as an easy rollback and as a substitute for backups. What is the biggest problem?
opts: Snapshots cannot be created while the virtual machine is running
Snapshots are encrypted so that nobody can restore from them
A snapshot always deletes the original virtual disk when it is created, so a second copy is needed first
Snapshots are not backups, can hold secrets and degrade performance, so they should be short-lived
why: A snapshot depends on the original storage, may contain memory and credentials and slows the guest as it grows, so it supports short-term rollback only. Snapshots can be taken while running, they do not delete the original disk and they are restorable.

q: Ransomware encrypts the file servers and then tries to reach the deduplicating backup appliance with the same domain credentials. Which design choice BEST protects backups?
opts: Using the domain administrator account for all backup jobs for simplicity
Immutable retention lock on the appliance, separate credentials and an isolated copy
Turning on thin provisioning so that more backups fit into the space
Mapping the backup appliance as a network drive on every file server
why: Immutability, separate credentials and an isolated copy stop ransomware from altering or deleting backups. Mapping the appliance everywhere and using domain admin credentials expose it, and thin provisioning affects capacity, not protection.

q: A cloud administrator notices that code running in a guest virtual machine has read memory belonging to another tenant's guest on the same host. Which threat is this?
opts: A phishing attack against the cloud provider's staff
A distributed denial of service attack on the host
A virtual machine escape or cross-VM side-channel attack
VM sprawl caused by too many unused machines
why: Crossing the isolation boundary between guests is a VM escape or side-channel attack. Sprawl is about unmanaged machines, phishing targets people and a denial of service attack aims at availability, not reading memory.

q: An attacker tries thousands of leaked passwords against a single public login page. Which pair of controls MOST directly stops the guessing from succeeding?
opts: Compressing network traffic and enabling a content delivery network
A longer web server log retention period and a faster storage array
Full-disk encryption on the web server and on its backups
Rate limiting or lockout together with multi-factor authentication
why: Throttling slows or stops online guessing, and a second factor makes a correct guessed password insufficient. Log retention, compression and disk encryption do not stop online login attempts.

q: A Kubernetes cluster's management API is reachable from the internet and accepts requests without authentication. What is the MOST serious consequence?
opts: Images in the registry will stop being scanned automatically
Individual containers will be unable to share the host kernel
An attacker can create and control workloads across the whole cluster
Pods will lose their ability to use network policies
why: An unauthenticated orchestrator API gives full control over every workload. Containers still share the kernel, and image scanning and network policy configuration are separate controls that do not change just because the API is exposed.

q: An employee with legitimate access to customer records copies them to a personal cloud drive before resigning. Which combination BEST reduces this insider risk?
opts: A faster internet link so large transfers finish more quickly
Least privilege, data loss prevention on uploads and prompt removal of access on departure
Removing the logs of file access so that nobody can misuse them
More frequent password changes for every employee in the company
why: Limiting access, detecting and blocking uploads and removing access at departure target the exposure directly. Password rotation does nothing about authorized access, bandwidth is irrelevant and removing logs removes detection.

q: A workstation's antivirus shows green, but the SOC sees PowerShell launching from an office document and contacting an unfamiliar server. Which statement BEST explains the gap?
opts: Antivirus always detects every kind of malware, so the alert must be false
PowerShell cannot be abused by attackers on a patched system
Office documents are safe from malicious macros once they are saved
Signature scanning misses new or fileless activity, which behavioural detection can catch
why: Signature-based scanning depends on known patterns, whereas behavioural detection notices suspicious process chains. No scanner catches everything, PowerShell is a common attacker tool even on patched systems and macros in saved documents can still run.

q: A browser shows a certificate warning when a user visits the company's partner portal from a hotel network. What should the user do?
opts: Disable the browser's certificate checks so that the portal opens
Stop and report it, because the warning can indicate interception or a bad certificate
Accept the exception, because the hotel network is trusted by default
Reload the page repeatedly until the warning goes away
why: A warning can mean an on-path attacker or a misconfigured site, so the user should stop and report. Hotel networks are not trusted, turning off checks removes the protection and repeating the attempt does not fix the cause.

q: Which TWO are effective countermeasures against phishing and other social engineering? (Choose two.)
opts: Trusting any message that uses the company's logo and signature
Turning off spam filtering so that no genuine mail is blocked
Verifying payment or credential requests through a known, separate channel
Awareness training with a simple way to report suspicious messages
Responding quickly to urgent requests from senior staff to be helpful
why: Trained, empowered users and out-of-band verification defeat the pressure tactics attackers rely on. Logos and signatures are trivially copied, speed on urgent requests is what attackers want and removing filtering lets more lures through.

q: Which TWO statements about HIDS and HIPS are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: File integrity monitoring is a typical host-based detection function
A HIPS is a replacement for patching known vulnerabilities
Host-based systems cannot see activity inside encrypted sessions
A HIPS can block a suspicious action on the host, while a HIDS only alerts
A HIDS can monitor every device on the network from one host
why: Prevention adds blocking to detection, and integrity monitoring of files and settings is a core host function. A host agent covers its own host, sees decrypted activity locally and does not remove the need for patching.

q: Which TWO practices help secure virtual machines and the hypervisor? (Choose two.)
opts: Keep unused virtual machines running in case someone needs them
Patch the hypervisor and keep a minimal host configuration
Allow unrestricted device pass-through from host to guests
Place management interfaces on a separate network with MFA
Give every administrator the same shared hypervisor account
why: Patching, minimization and isolated, strongly authenticated management reduce the chance of escape and takeover. Shared accounts remove accountability, idle machines add unpatched exposure and open pass-through widens the attack surface.

q: Which TWO items should a cloud outsourcing contract cover? (Choose two.)
opts: Permission for the provider to use customer data for its own marketing
The customer's right to audit or obtain independent assurance reports
Return and certified destruction of customer data when the contract ends
A provider's right to change security controls without telling customers
An exclusion of any breach notification duty
why: Audit rights and end-of-contract data return and destruction give the customer assurance and an exit. Marketing use, unannounced control changes and no breach notice all weaken the customer's position.

q: Which TWO are sound practices for the use of mobile devices that access corporate data? (Choose two.)
opts: Keep corporate and personal data together with no separation at all
Allow any device to connect as long as the user knows the Wi-Fi password
Check compliance, such as root or jailbreak status, before granting access
Let users disable the lock screen so work is faster
Require device encryption and a passcode, enforced by device management
why: Encryption, a passcode and compliance checks form the baseline of mobile control. A Wi-Fi password says nothing about device health, mixing data defeats selective wipe and disabling the lock screen exposes everything on a lost device.

q: Which TWO controls MOST directly protect backups from ransomware? (Choose two.)
opts: Using the same administrator password for backup and production
Immutable or write-once retention on the backup repository
Keeping a single backup copy on the system that is backed up
An isolated or offline copy that production credentials cannot reach
Mounting the repository as a writable share on all servers
why: Immutability and isolation keep at least one clean copy out of the attacker's reach. A writable share, shared credentials and a single co-located copy let ransomware reach the backups too.

q: Which TWO describe a zero-day attack accurately? (Choose two.)
opts: The flaw is unknown to the vendor or unpatched when attacks begin
It can only be prevented by disconnecting from the internet
Signature-based antivirus reliably detects it from the first attack
It can only affect systems that have never been patched
Behaviour-based detection and virtual patching can reduce the risk
why: Without a patch or signature, defence relies on layers such as behavioural detection, segmentation and virtual patching. Signatures do not exist at first, disconnecting is not the only option and fully patched systems can still be hit by a zero-day.

q: A trapdoor is an undocumented entry point that developers leave in code, which can bypass normal authentication.
opts: True
False
why: Maintenance hooks left in production are trapdoors. Code review and integrity monitoring help to find them, and they differ from a backdoor planted by an attacker only in who put them there.

q: A worm needs a user to open an infected file before it can spread to another system.
opts: True
False
why: A worm spreads by itself across networks, usually through a vulnerable service. A virus or trojan depends on a user action.

q: Signature-based antivirus is sufficient protection against zero-day exploits.
opts: True
False
why: A zero-day has no signature when attacks begin, so layered defences such as behaviour-based detection, hardening and segmentation are needed.

q: A host-based firewall protects a laptop even when it is connected to an untrusted public network.
opts: True
False
why: The software firewall travels with the device and enforces policy wherever it is, unlike a perimeter firewall at the office.

q: A TPM and an HSM are the same thing, so either can be used as a shared key service for a certificate authority.
opts: True
False
why: A TPM secures keys and boot measurements for one device, while an HSM is a shared, tamper-resistant key service for servers, applications and certificate authorities.

q: With selective wipe, a company can remove its own data and apps from a personal phone without erasing the owner's photos.
opts: True
False
why: Containers and managed apps make it possible to wipe only the corporate part, which is why they suit BYOD.

q: A snapshot of a virtual machine is a complete replacement for a backup.
opts: True
False
why: Snapshots rely on the original storage and are meant for short-term rollback. Backups are independent copies kept elsewhere.

q: In a hybrid cloud, the weakest link between the private and public parts can lower the overall level of security.
opts: True
False
why: Identity, network and policy must be consistent across both parts, or the less protected side becomes the way in.

q: Under the shared responsibility model, a customer that leaves a cloud storage bucket public can blame the provider for the exposure.
opts: True
False
why: Configuration of the customer's own resources and data access settings is the customer's responsibility.

q: Vishing is a phishing attack carried out through voice calls.
opts: True
False
why: Phishing by email, smishing by text message and vishing by voice all use deception to get credentials or actions, and each is countered by verifying through a known channel.

q: A scanner flags a trojan on a workstation. Which sequence of actions BEST reflects containment and remediation?
opts: Isolate the host, remove the malware or rebuild the system, then reset credentials the malware could have seen
Delete the flagged file, leave the host on the network and reset nothing since the scanner removed the threat
Reset all user passwords first and keep the infected host connected so that its behaviour can be observed
Rebuild the host immediately and reconnect it, then isolate it only if the scanner flags the file again
why: Contain first so the malware cannot spread or call out, then remove or rebuild, then reset anything it might have captured. Deleting one file leaves persistence and stolen credentials in place, resetting passwords on a connected infected host lets the malware capture the new ones, and reconnecting before containment risks a second outbreak.

q: A pop-up on an employee's laptop claims that 14 viruses were found and tells the user to call a number and buy a cleaning tool. What is this, and what should the user do?
opts: A genuine alert from the operating system; call the number promptly to stop the infection from spreading
A logic bomb; restart the laptop repeatedly until the message no longer appears on the screen
A rootkit warning; run the downloaded tool as administrator so that it can reach the kernel
Scareware; close the page without calling or paying and report it so the laptop is scanned
why: Fake infection warnings that push a purchase or call are scareware, so the user should not engage and should report it for a trusted scan. A genuine alert would not ask for a call or payment, running an unknown tool as administrator gives it full control, and a logic bomb is a condition-triggered payload.

q: An investigator finds a keylogger that has been sending an employee's typed credentials to an unknown server for weeks. What is the BEST remediation?
opts: Change the passwords from the infected machine so that the attacker loses access
Install a second antivirus product next to the first and keep the system running
Delete the keylogger and keep using the same passwords once the scan reports clean
Isolate and rebuild the machine, then reset the credentials from a known-clean device
why: Spyware may leave persistence behind, so the host is rebuilt, and credentials must be changed from a clean device because the infected one would expose the new ones. Keeping old passwords or changing them on the infected machine hands them to the attacker, and a second scanner does not prove the system is clean.

q: Scareware is malware or a fake alert that frightens users into buying useless software or installing something harmful.
opts: True
False
why: It works through fear and urgency, so awareness and a simple way to report it are the best defences, along with blocking known-bad sites.

q: A snapshot taken before patching gives a quick way to roll back, as long as it is deleted once the change is confirmed.
opts: True
False
why: Snapshots suit short-term rollback. Kept for long they slow the guest, may hold memory contents and secrets, and do not replace a tested backup.
